# Databases — inside the engine

> An interactive 3D cross-section of two database servers on one floor, each in its
> own wireframe cage. You orbit them, double-tap any part to fly to it, and open its
> card to read what that part actually does. Nothing is a screenshot: every block,
> packet, page and key is simulated, and the labels are the real structures.

The point of the project is the notation. A solid outline is a real volume of
something; a dashed one is a drawing of a structure that has no such footprint.
A pulse means a unit of work touched that block. Small maps of memory (shared
buffers, wal_buffers, aof_buf) float above the disk blocks they become.

## Paths

- `/` — the landing page (both cages).
- `/postgresql`, `/redis` — one cage each, from the same house shot.
- `/postgresql/<subject>` and `/redis/<subject>` — a named shot of one thing.
  `?db-panel=postgresql|redis` opens that engine's card; the path does not.

PostgreSQL subjects: `disk`, `tables`, `wal`, `wal-buffers`, `buffers`, `locks`,
`dev-shm`, `os-cache`, `pipeline`, `maintenance-work`, `pgsql-tmp`, `free-space`, `pages`,
`autovacuum`, `table-users`, `table-products`, `table-metrics`.

Redis subjects: `keys`, `skew`, `zset`, `hash`, `list`, `disk`, `aof`, `pubsub`.

## What is in it

PostgreSQL: parser and rewriter → planner → executor; shared buffers as 8 kB pages
with dirty state and the clock sweep; table runs and their pages, dead tuples, free
space; autovacuum as a drone walking the heap (it reclaims space inside pages and
never shrinks the file); the WAL run on disk with wal_buffers above it waiting for
fsync; backend ports, one process per connection, each with its input buffer.

The three memory facts a pool does not explain: `/dev/shm` with one dynamic shared
memory segment per parallel query (its tmpfs size is a hard limit, not a slowdown), the
OS page cache the planner is told about through `effective_cache_size` (a number, and
nothing is allocated for it), and `maintenance_work_mem` — a companion that rides the
autovacuum drone and is visible only while a job runs, holding one plate per heap page
with dead tuples to revisit: addresses, never pages. `pgsql_tmp` is the opposite and
gets its own dashed cage: disk, where a sort that outgrows the budget writes sorted
runs as BLCKSZ pages (empty here — nothing in this scene spills).

Locks are their own structure: a dashed rack beside the shared buffers, one block per
locked object with a pip per backend holding it, coloured by mode and tethered to the
relation it protects, with a queue of backends parked outside when the mode they want
does not share. The `locks` story walks three readers sharing one entry, an `ALTER TABLE`
waiting behind them, the commit that lets it through, and then a row lock that never
touches the rack at all.

Index lookups are stories rather than scenery: a statement physically walks socket →
parser → planner → executor, then descends a B-tree, a GIN, a BRIN or a hash index
whose pages ride above the packet as a dashed companion, then reads the heap page it
was pointed at — from disk when cold, from a buffer slot when warm — and goes back out
of the socket it came in on.

Redis: one command thread with a command queue and the epoll fd set under it; the
keyspace over the bucket array, including an incremental rehash; three deliberately
large values (a 1.4 M-member sorted set, a 5.3 M-field hash, a 2.1 M-element list)
and the handful of hot keys taking the traffic; encodings and when they convert;
pub/sub, where a subscribed socket is violet and PUBLISH stops at the loop and fans
out to those sockets without touching a key or the log; the AOF being appended, the
RDB base file, and the forked BGSAVE and AOF-rewrite children.
